title: A tri-scale in silico framework integrating pharmacovigilance and mechanistic modeling suggests tepotinib-associated acute kidney injury risk

paragraphs.en: Acute kidney injury (AKI), characterized by a rapid decline in renal function, poses a substantial global health burden due to its high incidence and strong association with poor clinical outcomes [1,2]. In critical care settings, AKI affects more than half of all patients and is independently linked to mortality rates exceeding 50% [3]. The prognostic significance of AKI is further evidenced by its association with increased short-term mortality, even for cases at the lower end of the severity spectrum [4]. A major barrier to effective management is the high rate of underdiagnosis; in large hospital systems, over 70% of AKI cases are missed, leading to delayed interventions and worsened patient prognosis [5–7]. This challenge is particularly acute in oncology. Severe AKI, defined and staged by the Kidney Disease: Improving Global Outcomes (KDIGO) clinical practice guidelines (corresponding to stage 2 or higher), is a frequent complication among cancer patients, often necessitating renal replacement therapy (RRT) and frequently leading to dose reduction or discontinuation of essential anticancer agents [8,9]. Consequently, the early prediction and prevention of drug-induced AKI have become a critical priority in the clinical management of vulnerable populations such as cancer patients [10,11].

The expanding arsenal of molecularly targeted therapies has markedly improved oncological outcomes yet simultaneously unveiled a spectrum of organ-specific toxicities, with nephrotoxicity emerging as a no7dose-limiting challenge for several kinase inhibitors (KIs) [12,13]. Tepotinib, a highly selective MET tyrosine kinase inhibitor (TKI), exemplifies this paradox by demonstrating robust efficacy in non-small cell lung cancer (NSCLC) with MET alterations, alongside a poorly defined renal safety profile [14]. A critical knowledge gap persists between its well-characterized pulmonary toxicity and the mechanistic obscurity surrounding its potential to induce AKI. Mechanistic insights remain limited as to whether the potential nephrotoxicity of tepotinib originates from on-target MET inhibition or results from promiscuous off-target engagements with kinases vital for renal homeostasis, leaving the implicated apoptotic or inflammatory pathways wholly unexplored [15]. Epidemiologically, the evidence is equally sparse, confined to anecdotal reports without any systematic, large-scale pharmacovigilance analysis to quantify the discrete AKI risk signal in real-world populations [16]. This dual ambiguity—spanning molecular pathogenesis and population-level evidence—significantly impedes the formulation of predictive biomarkers, evidence-based monitoring protocols, and effective risk-mitigation strategies for patients undergoing treatment with this promising agent.

Conventional unimodal analytical approaches are inherently inadequate to address this knowledge gap. While spontaneous reporting systems can detect safety signals, they lack mechanistic insight [17]; computational predictions like network toxicology propose system-wide interaction hypotheses but cannot validate specific binding events [18]; and molecular docking assesses binding affinity yet often ignores the broader physiological context [19]. While computational toxicology strategies integrating multiple methods are emerging for safety assessment, a critical methodological gap remains: the absence of a structured, tri-scale in silico framework explicitly designed to be generalizable for the proactive prediction of drug-induced nephrotoxicity [20,21]. This challenge resonates with the broader vision of digital toxicology initiatives, which advocate for the integration of multi-scale computational data to proactively de-risk drug development [22]. Current integrated approaches often lack the systematic, causal-evidence loop that spans from population-level signals down to molecular-scale binding validation, a capability particularly needed for de-risking novel oncology therapies. To address this knowledge gap, we developed and applied the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline, a named conceptual framework for predictive drug safety analytics. This pipeline was executed in the present study via the Tri-Scale Digital Nephrotoxicity Integrated Framework (TS-DNIF), which integrates (1) population-scale pharmacovigilance signal extraction to quantify the real-world risk, (2) network toxicology-based multi-target exploration to decipher the global target-pathway interactions and pinpoint central hub targets, and (3) mechanistic docking-based molecular plausibility assessment to rigorously validate the postulated interactions at the molecular level. This integrated approach creates an iterative analytical loop that transforms isolated data points into a coherent causal hypothesis. It first employs systematic mining of the FDA Adverse Event Reporting System (FAERS) to quantify the real-world AKI risk signal through robust disproportionality analysis [23]. These clinical signals then directly inform the subsequent network toxicology analysis, which deciphers the global target-pathway interactions between tepotinib and AKI to identify central hub targets and perturbed biological mechanisms. Finally, the postulated interactions between tepotinib and the prioritized hub targets are rigorously validated at the molecular scale using molecular docking, thereby bridging the gap between epidemiological observation and structural mechanism [24]. The unique power of this framework lies in its convergent validation: clinical data pinpoints the phenomenon, network analysis generates the mechanistic hypothesis, and structural biology assesses its physical plausibility, thereby delivering a unified explanation spanning from population-level evidence to molecular-scale interactions. Accordingly, this study introduces and applies the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline as a generalizable tri-scale framework for de-risking drug-induced organ toxicity, employing tepotinib-associated AKI as a specific case study to systematically assemble a causally coherent model from population-level risk to molecular-scale mechanism. Thereby, this study demonstrates the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline as a reusable workflow for evaluating TKI-induced nephrotoxicity, whose modular design provides a blueprint directly applicable to other MET and EGFR inhibitors, such as capmatinib and osimertinib, for mechanistic safety investigation. This demonstrates the framework’s utility in generating testable hypotheses for the off-target toxicity profiles of a wide range of targeted therapies beyond the present case study.

This study provides the first integrated pharmacovigilance, network toxicology and molecular docking-based analysis establishing a concrete association between tepotinib and AKI risk. By integrating disparate data modalities, it forges a novel mechanistic hypothesis: tepotinib perturbs renal homeostasis through coordinated interactions with a defined set of six core targets—HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC—thereby dysregulating pivotal survival and stress-response pathways, namely PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling. This hypothesis is uniquely scaffolded by a coherent evidentiary chain, from the significant real-world risk signal detected in FAERS, through the system-level pathway identification via network toxicology, to the atomic-scale confirmation of binding feasibility by molecular docking. The principal contribution lies in transforming isolated observations into an integrated, testable model that explicates tepotinib’s nephrotoxic potential across molecular, pathological, and clinical dimensions.

These findings bear immediate clinical relevance, underscoring the imperative for vigilant renal function monitoring in tepotinib-treated patients to enable early AKI detection and management. Consequently, patients receiving tepotinib may benefit from enhanced renal monitoring protocols aligned with KDIGO guidelines, including early and serial assessment of serum creatinine to enable timely intervention [9]. Beyond this specific drug-safety concern, the study establishes a generalizable methodological paradigm. The successful application of this sequential, multi-scale analytics framework demonstrates its utility for de-risking the development of complex targeted therapies by proactively elucidating off-target toxicities, thereby contributing to the advancement of safer precision oncology.

sections.title: Overall workflow of the tri-scale framework

paragraphs.en: This study was conducted following the three-tier TS-DNIF pipeline, which was executed by integrating population-scale pharmacovigilance signal extraction, network toxicology-based multi-target exploration, and mechanistic docking-based molecular plausibility assessment. The workflow commences with the quantification of real-world safety signals, which then directly inform the system-level identification of drug-disease interaction networks, and culminates in atomic-scale validation of the most pivotal interactions. The overall strategy is schematically summarized in Figure 1, delineating the sequential workflow from pharmacovigilance mining and network mapping to mechanistic docking.

sections.title: FAERS data acquisition and ADE screening

paragraphs.en: This study utilized data sourced from the FAERS database, an internationally recognized open drug safety surveillance platform that aggregates spontaneous adverse events (AEs) reports from global consumers, healthcare providers, and pharmaceutical entities. Post-market full-cycle monitoring data (2020–2025) were selected based on tepotinib’s FDA approval timeline, encompassing the complete temporal spectrum of drug safety signals. Raw data were downloaded in American Standard Code for Information Interchange (ASCII) report format, comprising adverse drug events (ADEs) reports designating tepotinib as the primary suspect medication. Ultimately, an analytical dataset was constructed containing key variables such as report date, patient age and gender, reporter type, and geographic region.

Drug nomenclature was standardized using Medex UIMA 1.3.8 [25], and adverse reaction terminology was classified and coded according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities (MedDRA) 26.1 standard [26], which organizes reports into hierarchical categories: Standardized MedDRA Organ Classes (SOCs) representing organ systems, and Preferred Terms (PTs) describing specific AEs. A strict data-cleaning protocol was applied to maintain data integrity and consistency by detecting and purging duplicate records with the most recent entries prioritized for identical CASEIDs, correcting outliers, and formatting fields uniformly [27]. Following preprocessing, the dataset comprised 8,137,279 demonstration reports, encompassing 37,236,725 drug cases and 20,670,887 REAC (coded AEs) records (Figure 2). Statistical analyses were performed using R software (version 4.4.2) and data flow diagrams were visualized via draw.io.

In this study, the reporting odds ratios (RORs) from disproportionality analysis was employed to evaluate ADE signals. To ensure result comprehensiveness and accuracy, gender stratification was conducted to separately assess ROR values in male and female populations. The utility of ROR resides in its capacity to correct biases arising from low reporting frequencies of specific events. Compared to ROR, the advantage of the Proportional Reporting Ratio (PRR) is its higher specificity. This study employed both ROR and PRR methods to leverage their respective strengths, aiming to detect more reliable safety signals. ROR and PRR were calculated according to Table 1, with a positive ADE signal defined as meeting all the following criteria: a ≥ 3, ROR 95% CI (lower limit) > 1, and PRR 95% CI (lower limit) > 1. Higher values of ROR and PRR indicate a stronger ADE signal intensity [28].

In this study, computational toxicology techniques were employed to predict the toxicity of tepotinib. The compound’s canonical SMILES structure code (CN1CCC(CC1)COC2 = CN = C(N = C2)C3 = CC = CC(=C3)CN4C(=O)C = CC(=N4)C5 = CC = CC(=C5)C#N) was retrieved from the PubChem database (https://pubchem.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/). Subsequently, systematic evaluations were carried out using the ProTox 3.0 (https://tox.charite.de/protox3/) and ADMETlab 2.0 (https://admetmesh.scbdd.com) prediction platforms.

To synthesize the predictions from ProTox 3.0 and ADMETlab 2.0, a standardized harmonization scheme was implemented. Integrated outcomes were categorized according to the following criteria: a result was designated as negative (-) in cases of inter-platform agreement or a single negative prediction with insufficient supplementary data; as positive (+) for a single positive prediction with a probability score between 0.3–0.7, or when positive evidence was prioritized in cases of conflicting results; and as consensus positive (++) for dual positive predictions from both platforms or a single positive prediction with a probability score ≥ 0.7. This integrative strategy established a consolidated and reliable toxicity profile for tepotinib.

To comprehensively identify the potential action targets of tepotinib, data from multiple databases were integrated in this study. First, based on the canonical SMILES code obtained, known targets were retrieved from the ChEMBL database (https://www.ebi.ac.uk/chembl/) with Homo sapiens specified as the species. Subsequently, the SMILES sequence was simultaneously submitted to the STITCH (http://stitch.embl.de/) and SwissTargetPrediction (http://www.swisstargetprediction.ch/) platforms for complementary target prediction, aiming to uncover potentially overlooked interacting targets. After cross-validating the prediction results of the three databases, the UniProt database (https://www.uniprot.org/) was utilized to standardize the target names. Then, data from multiple platforms were combined, and nonspecific targets were filtered out. Finally, a structurally complete and data – consistent target dataset was established.

This study integrated resources from three authoritative databases: GeneCards (https://www.genecards.org/), OMIM (https://www.omim.org/), and the Therapeutic Target Database (TTD, https://db.idrblab.net/ttd/). These databases contain large-scale multi-omics data on the associations between human genes and genetic diseases, enabling systematic screening of potential key targets in AKI. During data processing, differentiated screening strategies were applied based on database-specific characteristics. For GeneCards, a strict screening threshold of ‘Relevance score > 10’ was imposed using its quantitative evaluation metrics. As OMIM and TTD lack quantitative scoring systems, their raw search results were retained to ensure data integrity. A Venn diagram was then employed to analyze and identify overlapping targets between tepotinib’s action targets and AKI-related targets, with intersecting nodes designated as potential drug targets for AKI intervention. The remaining 3,243 targets (3,416 − 173) represent AKI-specific pathological factors not directly modulated by tepotinib, while the 198 tepotinib-exclusive targets (371 − 173) reflect non-renal pharmacological actions; both were excluded from further mechanistic analysis. This approach prioritizes targets with direct drug-disease interaction for network construction, ensuring biological relevance. Following systematic target analysis, an interaction network between tepotinib and AKI was constructed to characterize its multi-target action profile. Additionally, Cytoscape (version 3.10.0) was utilized to visualize a compound-target-disease network based on the curated target information.

sections.title: Construction of protein–protein interaction networks and screening of core targets

paragraphs.en: To characterize the drug-target interaction network, common action genes of tepotinib and AKI were submitted to the STRING online platform (https://cn.string-db.org/), with species restricted to Homo sapiens. A medium confidence threshold (>0.4) was applied to filter protein-protein interaction (PPI) relationships, and disconnected nodes were removed from the network visualization. Following acquisition of preliminary interaction data, Cytoscape was employed to construct a PPI network diagram, with node connectivity parameters calculated using the software’s built-in algorithms. Additionally, core targets of tepotinib in AKI were identified using a threshold of degree value > twice the median [29].

Functional enrichment analysis was carried out using the clusterProfiler package in R. Target gene identifiers were standardized via the org.Hs.eg.db human gene annotation database. The stringr package was employed for differential gene expression data cleaning, aiming to systematically dissect the molecular mechanisms underlying tepotinib’s effects on AKI. Gene Ontology (GO) analysis encompassed three functional domains: biological process (BP), molecular function (MF), and cellular component (CC). A dual-significance threshold was applied (p-value < 0.05; false discovery rate (FDR)-adjusted p-value < 0.05, based on the Benjamini–Hochberg method), with the top 10 significantly enriched terms retained for each subclass according to adjusted p-value ranking. The gene ratio, defined as the proportion of genes enriched in each term relative to the total number of input genes, was also reported for each result. For Kyoto Encyclopedia of Genes and Genomes (KEGG) pathway analysis, the top 30 enriched pathways were selected. Multidimensional visualizations were generated using the ggplot2, ggpubr, and circlize R packages, intuitively illustrating how the drug regulates disease phenotypes through coordinated BP-signaling pathway interactions.

In this study, the top six key targets ranked by degree value were selected for molecular docking validation with tepotinib. The SDF structure file of tepotinib was first retrieved from PubChem. Core target protein structures in Protein Data Bank (PDB) format were then downloaded from the RCSB PDB database (https://www.rcsb.org/) using their UniProt IDs. Docking analyses were performed using the CB-Dock2 platform (https://cadd.labshare.cn/cb-dock2/), which integrates CurPocket curvature-based cavity detection with AutoDock Vina. The platform automatically performs ligand and target protein hydrogenation, dehydration, energy optimization, and structure minimization, then identifies large surface cavities as potential binding sites to generate multiple docking conformations. CB-Dock2 selects the docking pose with the lowest Vina score, calculates binding energy, and generates 3D visualizations of binding modes to systematically characterize molecular interactions between tepotinib and core target proteins. These docking results predict potential binding interactions, which serve to prioritize targets for further investigation into functional inhibition.

A total of 555 AE reports associated with tepotinib were analyzed from the FAERS database, spanning from 2020 to 2025. The cohort was predominantly elderly, with 72.43% of patients aged 65 years or older. Sex distribution was balanced, with females comprising 51.89% of reports and males 44.86%. Reports were primarily submitted by physicians (43.60%) and consumers (37.66%), while pharmacists accounted for 14.23%. Geographically, the United States contributed the highest number of reports (46.13%), followed by Japan (24.68%). Oral administration was reported in 35.50% of cases. Serious outcomes included other significant events (37.87%), death (32.94%) and hospitalization (27.22%). These demographic and clinical patterns are detailed in Table 2.

Comprehensive disproportionality analysis of tepotinib-associated AEs identified 20 SOCs with significant signals (Table 3). Renal and urinary disorders demonstrated the most robust signal (ROR = 3.32, 95% CI: 2.67–4.13; PRR = 3.18, 95% CI: 2.56–3.95). This was followed by ear and labyrinth disorders (ROR = 2.13, 95% CI: 1.23–3.68; PRR = 2.12, 95% CI: 1.22–3.67) and metabolism and nutrition disorders (ROR = 2.04, 95% CI: 1.57–2.65; PRR = 2.00, 95% CI: 1.55–2.58). Furthermore, significant signals were evident in the respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal (ROR = 1.91, 95% CI: 1.59–2.29; PRR = 1.83, 95% CI: 1.53–2.18), general disorders and administration site conditions (ROR = 1.90, 95% CI: 1.70–2.12; PRR = 1.63, 95% CI: 1.51–1.76), and gastrointestinal disorders (ROR = 1.69, 95% CI: 1.45–1.97; PRR = 1.60, 95% CI: 1.39–1.84). Additionally, positive associations were observed for hepatobiliary disorders (ROR = 1.73, 95% CI: 1.14–2.64; PRR = 1.72, 95% CI: 1.14–2.60) and investigations (ROR = 1.38, 95% CI: 1.14–1.67; PRR = 1.35, 95% CI: 1.13–1.61).

At the PT level, several high-strength signals were detected (Table 4). Respiratory, thoracic and mediastinal disorders were prominently represented, with signals for pulmonary toxicity (ROR = 42.67, 95% CI: 22.14–82.26; PRR = 42.41, 95% CI: 22.21–80.98), organizing pneumonia (ROR = 21.37, 95% CI: 6.88–66.41; PRR = 21.33, 95% CI: 6.84–66.48), and pneumothorax (ROR = 13.12, 95% CI: 5.45–31.57; PRR = 13.07, 95% CI: 5.41–31.57). Among renal and urinary disorders, renal impairment (ROR = 20.60, 95% CI: 15.25–27.81; PRR = 20.01, 95% CI: 14.91–26.85) and toxic nephropathy (ROR = 14.19, 95% CI: 5.31–37.87; PRR = 14.15, 95% CI: 5.31–37.7) were significant. Within investigations, notable signals were observed for blood albumin decreased (ROR = 30.69, 95% CI: 11.49–81.97; PRR = 30.61, 95% CI: 11.49–81.56) and blood creatinine increased (ROR = 16.80, 95% CI: 11.13–25.38; PRR = 16.56, 95% CI: 10.97–24.99). For general disorders and administration site conditions, edema constituted the most prominent signal (ROR = 44.02, 95% CI: 32.90–58.88; PRR = 42.63, 95% CI: 32.40–56.09). Additionally, strong associations were identified in metabolism and nutrition disorders for hypoalbuminaemia (ROR = 46.71, 95% CI: 23.29–93.68; PRR = 46.45, 95% CI: 23.39–92.24) and in neoplasms benign, malignant and unspecified (incl cysts and polyps) for malignant pleural effusion (ROR = 87.93, 95% CI: 28.23–273.91; PRR = 87.75, 95% CI: 28.15–273.50). Other notable signals included lymphoedema (ROR = 32.88, 95% CI: 14.73–73.37; PRR = 32.75, 95% CI: 14.66–73.15), infectious pleural effusion (ROR = 67.13, 95% CI: 21.57–208.93; PRR = 66.99, 95% CI: 21.49–208.79), and hepatotoxicity (ROR = 8.39, 95% CI: 3.48–20.18; PRR = 8.36, 95% CI: 3.46–20.20).

Integrated computational toxicological evaluation using ProTox 3.0 and ADMETlab 2.0 predicted that tepotinib has the potential to cause neurotoxicity, respiratory toxicity and cardiotoxicity. Computational prediction also suggests potential hepatotoxicity and nephrotoxicity. Furthermore, in silico models predicted that tepotinib may possess carcinogenic, cytotoxic and mutagenicity. In contrast, skin sensitization was not predicted to pose a substantial risk. These computational findings highlight the importance of dosage optimization in the therapeutic use of tepotinib (Table 5).

sections.title: Integrated analysis of tepotinib targets and AKI-related genes

paragraphs.en: This study systematically examined tepotinib’s potential targets in AKI using a multi‐source data integration approach. Initially, drug target databases such as ChEMBL, STITCH and SwissTargetPrediction were queried to screen 371 molecular targets potentially interacting with tepotinib. Concurrently, 3,416 disease genes closely associated with AKI pathological processes were retrieved from disease databases including GeneCards, OMIM and TTD. Through data cleansing and cross-comparison analysis, 173 common targets of significant research value were ultimately identified, constituting a key molecular network through which tepotinib might modulate AKI pathological processes. Visual analysis using a Venn diagram intuitively illustrated the intersection between tepotinib targets and AKI-related genes, offering novel research directions for in-depth exploration of its mechanism of action (Figure 3(a)). Additionally, a compound-target-disease network was depicted in Figure 3(b). The target database established in this study not only unveils the potential molecular basis of drug action but also provides an important foundation for subsequent functional validation and mechanistic investigation.

sections.title: Interaction networks of potential targets and identification of core genes

paragraphs.en: A PPI network was constructed using the STRING database (Figure 4), consisting of 173 nodes and 1,953 interaction edges with an average node degree of 22.6. The TSV-format data were then imported into Cytoscape for visual optimization. Leveraging built-in topological analysis algorithms with a threshold of degree value > twice the median, 23 core targets associated with tepotinib’s regulation of AKI were identified. A dedicated PPI network (Figure 5) was generated to visualize interactions among these core targets. Notably, the three most critical targets ranked by degree values were HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC, underscoring their hub roles in network information transmission. Topological properties were computed using the software’s Analyze Network function (Table 6).

sections.title: Pathway enrichment analysis of core targets

paragraphs.en: GO enrichment analysis revealed that tepotinib’s intervention in AKI is achieved through multidimensional regulation of BP, CC and MF (Figure 6). At the BP level, significantly enriched pathways included positive regulation of protein phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 7.21 × 10–31; gene ratio = 0.26), peptidyl-serine phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 1.23 × 10–33; gene ratio = 0.20) and peptidyl-tyrosine phosphorylation (adjusted p-value = 1.26 × 10–23; gene ratio = 0.17). CC analysis revealed significant enrichment of membrane raft (adjusted p-value = 7.82 × 10–14; gene ratio = 0.13) and membrane microdomain (adjusted p-value = 7.84 × 10–14; gene ratio = 0.13), along with enrichment of transferase complex, transferring phosphorus-containing groups (adjusted p-value = 1.36 × 10–23; gene ratio = 0.18). At the MF level, significant enrichment was observed for protein serine/threonine kinase activity (adjusted p-value = 3.44 × 10–76; gene ratio = 0.44), transmembrane receptor protein kinase activity (adjusted p-value = 5.91 × 10–22; gene ratio = 0.12) and transmembrane receptor protein tyrosine kinase activity (adjusted p-value = 7.06 × 10–18; gene ratio = 0.09).

KEGG enrichment analysis delineated the core molecular mechanisms through which tepotinib modulates AKI pathogenesis (Figure 7). Significantly enriched pathways included the MAPK signaling pathway (adjusted p-value = 7.12 × 10–38; gene ratio = 0.26), PI3K-Akt signaling pathway (adjusted p-value = 6.64 × 10–26; gene ratio = 0.22), Calcium signaling pathway (adjusted p-value = 1.03 × 10–26; gene ratio = 0.19), Ras signaling pathway (adjusted p-value = 6.00 × 10–27; gene ratio = 0.19), Focal adhesion (adjusted p-value = 2.72 × 10–19; gene ratio = 0.15) and Toll-like receptor signaling pathway (adjusted p-value = 1.65 × 10–19; gene ratio = 0.11).

The selection of enriched GO terms and KEGG pathways was stringently filtered based on both statistical significance and relevance to core pathophysiological processes of AKI, particularly inflammation, fibrosis and metabolic dysregulation. This integrated omics approach ensured alignment between robust statistical evidence and potential clinical mechanisms, with deliberate emphasis on therapeutically actionable molecular targets. Collectively, these findings establish a validated mechanistic foundation for elucidating tepotinib’s role in AKI pathogenesis.

Table 7 compiles detailed molecular docking results between tepotinib and six core targets: HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC. Automated analysis via the CB-Dock2 platform revealed binding free energies ranging from −10.6 to −8.0 kcal/mol. A binding energy below 0 kcal/mol indicates molecular binding activity, with lower values reflecting stronger interactions. In this study, all energy values far exceeded the strong binding threshold of −5.0 kcal/mol, fully demonstrating highly spontaneous and stable interactions between tepotinib and these targets. Figure 8 depicts the lowest-energy conformation in three dimensions, highlighting key amino acid residues participating in hydrogen bond formation. These findings prioritize the six core targets and provide a structural rationale for their potential role in tepotinib-associated AKI.

Employing a triangulated approach that integrates pharmacovigilance, network toxicology and molecular docking, this study generates the first systematic, hypothesis-generating evidence investigating the association between tepotinib and AKI. Mining of the FAERS database revealed a significant signal for renal and urinary disorders at the SOC level (ROR = 3.32). Most critically, at the PT level, a potent signal was detected for renal impairment (ROR = 20.60), which is a primary clinical descriptor for AKI. While other significant signals (e.g. pulmonary toxicity) were observed, this analysis focuses on deciphering the mechanism underlying the robust AKI signal. Computational toxicological profiling provided preliminary support, suggesting a potential nephrotoxic risk as per in silico models. To specifically elucidate the pathogenesis of AKI, a network toxicology framework was implemented, identifying 173 shared targets between tepotinib and AKI. Topological analysis of the protein-interaction network further pinpointed six central hub targets—HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC—suggesting their pivotal roles in the potential pathogenesis. Functional enrichment analysis of these hub targets revealed their profound involvement in critical pathways central to renal injury, most notably the PI3K-Akt (adjusted p-value = 6.64 × 10–26) and MAPK (adjusted p-value = 7.12 × 10–38) signaling pathways. Subsequent molecular docking predicted stable binding conformations between tepotinib and these hubs (Vina scores: −8.0 to −10.6 kcal/mol), thereby formulating a structural hypothesis for off-target interactions that could contribute to nephrotoxicity. This hypothesis, however, requires direct experimental validation to confirm functional inhibition [24,30]. Collectively, this synergistic application of computational methodologies constructs a coherent and mechanistically plausible hypothesis for tepotinib-induced AKI, underscoring the value of this integrative analytics framework in modern drug safety assessment. This approach establishes the first integrative application of FAERS-based signal detection linked to mechanistic docking, thereby providing a hypothesis-generating model for future toxicogenomic validation.

Building upon the integrated evidence from pharmacovigilance, computational toxicology and network analysis presented above, we propose a mechanistic hypothesis elucidating how tepotinib’s predicted multi-target engagement could contribute to the pathogenesis of AKI through interconnected signaling networks. This integrative mechanistic model is visually summarized in Figure 9.

The profound dysregulation of the PI3K-Akt and MAPK pathways—both critically involved in regulating renal tubular cell survival, inflammation, and apoptosis, which are pivotal processes in AKI pathogenesis—serves as the central axis of the proposed AKI mechanism, with the six hub targets functioning as critical nodal points that amplify and propagate the injury signals [31–34]. The specific pathophysiological consequences of this pathway dysregulation are twofold and critical to AKI progression. Suppression of the PI3K-Akt signaling pathway directly compromises renal tubular epithelial integrity, crippling essential survival signals and sensitizing cells to metabolic stress, which culminates in the acute tubular necrosis that defines clinical AKI [35]. In parallel, hyperactivation of the MAPK signaling pathway orchestrates a damaging inflammatory cascade within the kidney, driving the release of cytokines, promoting leukocyte infiltration, and causing microvascular injury that further compromises renal function [36]. This dual assault of impaired cellular viability and amplified inflammation underpins the rapid functional decline observed in tepotinib-associated AKI [37]. The mechanistic cascade unfolds through a series of coordinated perturbations. Within this model, putative inhibition of AKT1 following its predicted binding could destabilize the core survival signaling axis, leading to reduced phosphorylation of downstream substrates [38]. This loss of AKT1 activity results in concomitant activation of GSK-3β and BAD, initiating mitochondrial outer membrane permeabilization and caspase-9 activation, thereby establishing a robust pro-apoptotic environment in renal tubular cells [39–41]. Simultaneously, the inflammatory milieu created by TNF stabilization promotes sustained JNK activation through MAP2K4/MAP2K7 phosphorylation, which in turn drives AP-1-mediated transcription of profibrotic factors such as TGF-β1, which may contribute to maladaptive repair processes following acute injury [42,43]. This process is further amplified by SRC inhibition, which disrupts normal focal adhesion kinase signaling and impairs epithelial barrier function, creating a permissive environment for fibroblast activation and collagen deposition [44,45]. Notably, these pathways exhibit extensive crosstalk that creates feed-forward amplification loops. The oxidative stress generated through NADPH oxidase activation, evidenced by pathway enrichment, not only causes direct macromolecular damage but also inhibits PP2A activity, leading to enhanced JNK phosphorylation that further exacerbates the apoptotic signaling [46,47]. Meanwhile, HSP90AA1 inhibition serves as a critical amplifier by destabilizing multiple client proteins including AKT1 itself, SRC, and various MAPK pathway components, thereby sensitizing the entire network to tepotinib’s effects [48–50]. The consequent activation of the NLRP3 inflammasome in response to mitochondrial ROS release and potassium efflux leads to gasdermin-D-mediated pyroptosis, representing an additional cell death modality that fuels the inflammatory response [51–54]. This integrated model demonstrates how tepotinib’s polypharmacological profile precipitates the hallmark functional decline of AKI through the simultaneous disruption of survival, inflammatory, and repair pathways in renal cells. The convergence of apoptotic signaling, metabolic disruption, inflammatory activation, and impaired repair mechanisms—all stemming from coordinated multi-target engagement—provides a comprehensive explanation for the robust AKI signal detected in our FAERS analysis. The systems-level understanding achieved through this integrative approach not only proposes a plausible mechanism for tepotinib’s nephrotoxic potential but also establishes a framework for predicting and mitigating similar adverse effects in other KIs.

This established framework is inherently generalizable, as its tri-scale architecture is agnostic to the specific drug target. The foundational principle—that off-target toxicity arises from drug-protein interactions perturbing core physiological pathways—applies universally across targeted therapies. Consequently, the pipeline can be directly deployed to profile the safety of diverse TKIs, from investigating the renal effects of MET inhibitors such as crizotinib and capmatinib to delineating the hepatotoxicity profiles of multi-KIs including regorafenib and lenvatinib [55–58]. Its utility extends to other major drug classes: it can integrate the pharmacovigilance signals of immune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs), exemplified by anti-PD-1-associated pneumonitis, with immune pathway networks to propose causal mechanisms [59], and systematically explore the off-target toxicities of antibody-drug conjugates (ADCs), such as the ocular damage induced by tisotumab vedotin, by identifying candidate targets beyond the intended payload [60].

While this study focuses on tepotinib, the TS-DNIF pipeline is inherently scalable and can be extended to other oncologic agents, including MET inhibitors, EGFR inhibitors, immune checkpoint inhibitors, and antibody–drug conjugates. Future iterations could incorporate dynamic pathway weighting, time-resolved FAERS signal evolution, and integration into predictive dashboards or digital twin kidney injury simulations for real-time risk tracking.

This study provides the first multi-platform evidence establishing an elevated risk of AKI as a previously underrecognized safety concern of tepotinib, thereby expanding its documented safety profile beyond the well-characterized pulmonary toxicities [61]. Our integrated analysis reveals a critical distinction between the drug’s intended therapeutic mechanism and its adverse effect pattern, suggesting that AKI may represent an off-target toxicity rather than a consequence of its primary pharmacological action. The mechanistic plausibility of our findings is strengthened by their alignment with established renal pathophysiology. Indeed, the six hub genes we identified correspond to a syndicate of targets governing distinct aspects of kidney injury: HSP90AA1 in proteostasis [62], AKT1 in survival signaling [63], EGFR in reparative regeneration [64], CASP3 as the apoptosis executioner [65], TNF as a master inflammatory regulator [66], and SRC in glomerular integrity [67]—all with well-documented roles in AKI. This collective evidence strongly underpins their selection as central mediators. Building upon this foundational evidence, we next delineate their specific interplay within our proposed mechanistic model. AKT1 stands out for its well-documented role in renal cellular survival, particularly through maintaining mitochondrial membrane integrity under stress conditions [40]. Similarly, EGFR’s crucial function in promoting tubular repair following injury [68], and SRC’s involvement in preserving glomerular filtration barrier integrity [69], provide strong biological foundations for their putative roles in AKI pathogenesis. The remaining targets complete this pathological network: HSP90AA1 disruption potentially compromises cellular stress adaptation by affecting protein stability, TNF engagement may amplify inflammatory cascades, while CASP3 activation likely executes the final apoptotic steps [70–72]. This target network reveals the complexity of kinase inhibitor toxicity, suggesting that future drug development should incorporate comprehensive assessment of off-target interactions, particularly with renal protective pathways. Our findings indicate that toxicity profiles may emerge from distributed network perturbations rather than isolated pathway inhibition, highlighting the need for therapeutic strategies that balance efficacy with safety through improved target selectivity.

The findings from this integrated analysis extend beyond mechanistic elucidation to offer tangible translational implications across clinical practice, scientific research, and methodological innovation. From a clinical standpoint, the consistent signal of renal impairment indicative of AKI identified through both disproportionality analysis and computational toxicology highlights a previously underappreciated risk of AKI for tepotinib [73]. This evidence supports the advisability of incorporating enhanced AKI monitoring into clinical management protocols for patients undergoing tepotinib therapy, particularly among high-risk subgroups such as the elderly or those with preexisting renal compromise [74,75]. Regular assessment of serum creatinine, urinary albumin, and estimated glomerular filtration rate(eGFR) could facilitate the early detection of early renal function decline, enabling timely dose adjustment or intervention and potentially attenuating the progression to acute or chronic kidney disease [76–78]. For the research community, this study provides a strategically valuable set of high-priority molecular targets—HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC—and their associated pathways, which effectively refocuses the research agenda from broad screening to targeted validation [79]. This curated dataset offers a decisive starting point for mechanistic inquiries, substantially de-risking and accelerating the process of elucidating tepotinib’s AKI risk. It enables the field to concentrate resources on experimentally confirming the roles of these specific hubs in renal pathology, such as their collective impact on apoptosis, inflammation, and fibrosis within the kidney [80,81]. Moreover, this study lays a definitive foundation for pioneering research into the polypharmacological basis of kinase inhibitor toxicity, with the potential to inform the design of safer next-generation drugs or protective co-therapies that mitigate renal damage while preserving anticancer efficacy [82]. On a methodological level, our study provides a practical implementation of a digital toxicology framework, establishing the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline as a robust and generalizable paradigm for the systematic evaluation of drug safety. The sequential integration of pharmacovigilance analytics, network toxicology and structural biology creates a coherent, hypothesis-generating pipeline that translates complex data into biologically intelligible and clinically relevant insights [83–85]. Especially, this tri-scale in silico framework is not limited to nephrotoxicity assessment but holds promise as a versatile tool for proactively elucidating other serious AEs, such as cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity, or immune-related complications, across the expanding arsenal of targeted therapies. Capitalizing on this generalizable framework, our study specifically nominates the identified hub genes—AKT1, TNF, EGFR, HSP90AA1, SRC and CASP3—as a mechanistically grounded multi-target signature for predictive biomarker development. We propose that future research should prioritize the detection of their expression or protein products in urinary exosomes. As stable, kidney-derived vesicles rich in pathophysiological cargo, exosomes offer a potent, noninvasive source for an early-warning system [86,87]. Validating this signature could enable the detection of subclinical renal injury prior to overt functional decline, paving the way for preemptive interventions and personalized risk management in tepotinib-treated patients. This framework demonstrates how modern computational approaches can efficiently prioritize potential toxicities, offering a scalable strategy for the prospective safety assessment of novel therapeutics, especially those with complex polypharmacology. By bridging disparate data modalities, this approach represents a significant advancement in predictive toxicology, holding promise for enhancing the risk-benefit profile of targeted therapies and ultimately improving patient safety outcomes. To translate this potential into a structured strategy, we propose a comprehensive blueprint for AI-enabled predictive nephrotoxicity surveillance (Table 8).

Capitalizing on this integrative foundation, we propose a Composite Nephrotoxicity Predicted Risk Index (NPRI) as the logical next evolution of our framework. The NPRI would computationally integrate the core evidence dimensions identified in this study—namely ROR intensity, network centrality, docking scores, and AKI-pathway weighting—into a unified predictive metric. Future calibration of this index using machine learning on reference drug cohorts could enable prospective risk stratification and guide tailored renal monitoring for novel therapeutics. Validating the NPRI across federated clinical datasets would thus mark a critical advance toward proactive, data-driven drug safety assessment [88,89].

This analytical pipeline is also inherently positioned for integration with next-generation pharmacovigilance ecosystems. The translational potential of our tri-scale framework can be significantly amplified through strategic synergy with electronic health record (EHR) systems and federated AI networks. Specifically, the significant AKI signal and hub targets identified by our framework can direct a focused, hypothesis-driven interrogation of linked FAERS-EHR databases. This enables signal verification against robust clinical data, where EHRs provide the necessary context—such as longitudinal serum creatinine trends and competing nephrotoxic exposures—to adjust for confounding factors and strengthen causal inference [90,91]. Concurrently, our computationally derived multi-target hypothesis serves as a prior knowledge module within privacy-preserving federated AI networks, where the prioritized candidate targets and pathways are validated and refined across multiple institutions using federated learning on local EHR data [92]. This synergistic integration creates a self-reinforcing cycle of discovery and validation: the mechanistically grounded hypotheses generated by our framework guide targeted interrogation of real-world evidence, while insights derived from federated learning across diverse populations iteratively refine our understanding of drug toxicity mechanisms [93]. Ultimately, this integration establishes a closed-loop, proactive surveillance system for oncology drug safety.

The interpretations of this study should be considered in the context of its methodological framework. The pharmacovigilance findings are inherently constrained by the limitations of the FAERS database. Its voluntary nature introduces reporting biases, including the underreporting of mild events and potential overrepresentation of severe outcomes. Additionally, the structure of the MedDRA coding system may lead to the fragmentation or misclassification of complex clinical syndromes [94]. Most critically, the absence of controlled comparisons and comprehensive clinical data means that the detected signals, while significant, cannot establish definitive causality between tepotinib and AKI [95]. The computational approaches, while valuable for hypothesis generation, present complementary limitations. Network toxicology, by focusing on protein-coding genes, may overlook pathogenic contributions from non-coding RNAs, offering an incomplete mechanistic picture [18,96]. Furthermore, the current framework lacks dynamic modeling of the injury process over time. This is exemplified by molecular docking, which provides a static snapshot of binding affinity but cannot capture the time-dependent evolution of drug-target interactions or the subsequent biological cascades in a physiological setting, potentially oversimplifying the mechanism. Critically, the computational prediction of binding affinity, as performed here, is a necessary but insufficient condition for confirming functional biochemical inhibition of the identified targets [94,97]. Furthermore, as computational toxicology evolves to incorporate more complex, AI-driven predictive models, future studies would benefit from adhering to rigorous reporting standards such as the TRIPOD-AI statement [98]. To address these aspects, future investigations should prioritize several strategic directions. Experimental validation of the prioritized hub targets is essential, for example, by employing techniques such as Western blot to quantify tepotinib’s effect on the phosphorylation of key nodes like AKT1 and STAT3 in renal models [99]. Critically, to move beyond the associative evidence provided by pharmacovigilance and establish causal inference, prospective clinical studies with protocol-defined renal monitoring are indispensable. Prospective clinical studies evaluating dose-adjusted renal safety endpoints, such as eGFR slope, would substantiate the pharmacovigilance signals [100]. The integration of emerging technologies like single-cell transcriptomics could significantly enhance target discovery comprehensiveness by capturing cell-type-specific responses [101], while molecular dynamics simulations would provide critical insights into the stability of tepotinib-target interactions over time, moving beyond static models [102]. All in all, these efforts would establish a more robust foundation for precisely understanding and managing tepotinib’s renal effects.

In summary, through the application of our integrated computational framework, this study provides compelling evidence linking tepotinib to an elevated risk of AKI, elucidating a multi-target mechanistic hypothesis centered on the disruption of six core hubs—HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC—within critical pathways including PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling. The concordance of signals from pharmacovigilance analytics, network toxicology and molecular docking underscores the biological plausibility of this association. These findings highlight the need for vigilant AKI surveillance in clinical practice and establish a robust, data-driven foundation for subsequent research aimed at validating the proposed mechanisms and developing strategies to mitigate AKI risk while preserving the antitumor efficacy of tepotinib.

Collectively, by applying it to tepotinib, our work establishes a powerful, hypothesis-generating framework that translates multi-scale computational data into a testable model of drug-induced toxicity. This tripartite framework, which includes FAERS-derived signal detection, network toxicology-based hypothesis mapping, and molecular docking verification, may serve as a generalizable paradigm for early nephrotoxicity risk evaluation in targeted therapies.

This integrated analysis establishes a significant association between the MET inhibitor tepotinib and AKI. More importantly, it showcases the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline as a reusable, three-scale workflow for evaluating nephrotoxicity across the TKI drug class. Pharmacovigilance mining revealed a robust signal for renal impairment (ROR = 20.60). A convergent multi-scale approach further elucidated the mechanistic basis for this association, pinpointing a toxicity network centered on six hub targets—HSP90AA1, AKT1, EGFR, CASP3, TNF and SRC. These targets dysregulate critical renal pathways, including PI3K-Akt and MAPK signaling, an interaction model supported by computational evidence of high-affinity binding from molecular docking. Methodologically, this work presents the first application of the FAERS-NetDock Pipeline, linking FAERS-based signal detection to mechanistic docking via network toxicology. This approach provides a generalizable, hypothesis-generating model to guide future toxicogenomic studies. Consequently, patients receiving tepotinib may benefit from early serum creatinine monitoring and a comprehensive assessment of nephrotoxic risk factors. The FAERS-NetDock Pipeline exemplified here is generalizable for de-risking the development of targeted therapies. This tripartite model can be extended to screen for other off-target organ toxicities, such as cardiotoxicity, hepatotoxicity or immune-related AEs, in a wide range of targeted oncology agents. As demonstrated with tepotinib, the pipeline is directly applicable for the safety profiling of diverse TKIs, including crizotinib, capmatinib, savolitinib, afatinib, and osimertinib.
